summary: Explains how the reserved bits in the common header of PIM version 2 messages can be used by individual message types, and creates a registry to track that usage. It also extends the PIM message type space by defining three new message types that borrow some reserved bits as an extended type range. It was replaced by RFC 9436.

eli5.summary: Imagine a form with a few boxes left blank for later. This document says how those blank boxes can be used so the form can hold many more kinds of messages.

questions: what are the reserved bits in the pim header
how is the pim message type space extended
how many pim message types are there
subtitle: Gives the spare bits in every PIM message header a job, and uses some of them to stretch the message type space.

tldr.problem: All PIM version 2 messages share a common header with eight reserved bits, but no document said how individual message types may use them. The message type space, 0 to 15, was also almost exhausted.
tldr.mechanism: The reserved bits are renamed Flag Bits and are defined per message type, with a registry recording each type's usage. Types 13, 14 and 15 each use the top four Flag Bits as a Subtype, giving 48 extended types.
tldr.outcome: PIM gained room for future message types and a registry of flag bit usage. The document obsoletes RFC 6166 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 9436.

facts.label: Defined message types before this RFC
Flag bits left per extended type

today: RFC 8736 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9436, so that is the document to read for current practice. It obsoleted RFC 6166 and updated RFC 3973, RFC 5015, RFC 5059, RFC 6754, RFC 7761 and RFC 8364.

sections.title: Why the Reserved Bits Needed a Rule
sections.content:
PIM version 2 messages all start with a common header defined in RFC 7761. That header contains eight reserved bits, yet no document formally said these bits could be used separately by each message type.

This RFC calls those bits Flag Bits and says they are used on a per-message-type basis. It also notes that the defined message types run from 0 to 15, that this space is almost exhausted, and that type 15 had already been reserved for type space extension by RFC 6166, which this document obsoletes.
sections.eli5: A form had some empty boxes nobody was sure how to use. This paper says who may fill them in, and how.

sections.title: The Common PIM Header with Flag Bits
sections.content:
The common header keeps its layout: the PIM version, the message type, the eight-bit Flag Bits field (formerly Reserved) and the checksum. Only the Reserved field is renamed and redefined. All other fields remain unchanged.

To talk about single bits, the RFC numbers them from bit 7, the most significant and right after the Type field, down to bit 0, the one just before the Checksum.
sections.eli5: The top of every PIM message has a row of little boxes. This paper gives the boxes numbers so everyone can point to the same one.

sections.title: Flag Bit Definitions per Message Type
sections.content:
Unless a document says otherwise, all flag bits are Reserved: they MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored upon receipt. The specification of any new PIM type MUST say whether its bits are treated differently.

  • Type 4 (Bootstrap): bit 7 is No-Forward, defined in RFC 5059. The rest are reserved.
  • Type 10 (DF Election): bits 4 to 7 form a subtype, defined in RFC 5015. The rest are reserved.
  • Type 12 (PIM Flooding Mechanism): bit 7 is No-Forward, defined in RFC 8364. The rest are reserved.
  • Types 13, 14 and 15: defined by the type space extension.
sections.eli5: Unless a message says otherwise, its boxes stay empty and everyone ignores them. A few message kinds already have special uses for certain boxes.

sections.title: Extending the PIM Type Space
sections.content:
Types 13, 14 and 15 each get 16 subtypes, which gives 48 subtypes for future PIM extensions. The Subtype field is made from the four most significant flag bits (bits 4 to 7). The notation type.subtype, such as 13.0, names these extended types.

The four remaining flag bits (bits 0 to 3) are reserved for each extended type to use as it needs.
sections.eli5: Running out of message names is like running out of locker numbers. Now three lockers each get sixteen shelves, so there are many more places to put things.

sections.title: The Updated Message Types Registry
sections.content:
The IANA "PIM Message Types" registry is updated to show which flag bits each type uses, and it now references this document. The registration policy remains IETF Review, and new assignments MUST define any non-default flag bit usage along with the type.

Types 13.0 through 15.15 are listed as unassigned. Each extended type has only 4 flag bits available, and new extended types should be assigned consecutively, starting with 13.0, then 13.1, and so on. The RFC says it has no impact on security and no change to the considerations in RFC 7761 and RFC 3973.
sections.eli5: There is a big list of message kinds and what each box means. New kinds must say how they use the boxes, and the new shelves are handed out in order.

fields.name: Subtype
fields.desc: Flag bits 4 to 7 used as a subtype.

fields.name: FB
fields.desc: Flag bits 0 to 3, reserved for each extended type.
